---
<!-- ass-1: body_md -->
\label{asm:0} 
Denote $F_\star=\min_{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x})$ and suppose $F\left(\mathbf{x}^{1}\right)- F_\star \leq \Delta_{F}$ for the initial point $\mathbf{x}^{1}$.
<!-- end ass-1 -->
<!-- ass-2: body_md -->
\label{asm:1} 
All functions $f_1, \dotsc, f_T$ are $L_f$-Lipschitz continuous, and their gradients $\nabla f_1, \dotsc, \nabla f_T$ are also $L_J$-Lipschitz continuous.
<!-- end ass-2 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Under Assumption~\ref{asm:1}, the objective $F$ is $L_F$-smooth, where
$L_F \coloneqq L_f^{2T-1}L_J\sum_{i=1}^T{L_f^{-i}}$.
\begin{ass}\label{asm:stochastic2} 
The function and gradient estimates are unbiased with bounded variance, i.e.,
\begin{gather*}
       \mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[f_i(\mathbf{x};\xi)\right] = f_i(\mathbf{x}), \quad
	  \mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\nabla f_i(\mathbf{x};\xi)\right] = \nabla f_i(\mathbf{x}),\\
\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\left\|f_i(\mathbf{x};\xi) - f_i(\mathbf{x})\right\|^2 \right]\leq \sigma^2, \quad
	\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\left\|\nabla f_i(\mathbf{x};\xi) - \nabla f_i(\mathbf{x}) \right\|^2 \right] \leq  \sigma^2.
\end{gather*}
\end{ass}
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- ass-3: body_md -->
\label{asm:stochastic2} 
The function and gradient estimates are unbiased with bounded variance, i.e.,
\begin{gather*}
       \mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[f_i(\mathbf{x};\xi)\right] = f_i(\mathbf{x}), \quad
	  \mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\nabla f_i(\mathbf{x};\xi)\right] = \nabla f_i(\mathbf{x}),\\
\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\left\|f_i(\mathbf{x};\xi) - f_i(\mathbf{x})\right\|^2 \right]\leq \sigma^2, \quad
	\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\left\|\nabla f_i(\mathbf{x};\xi) - \nabla f_i(\mathbf{x}) \right\|^2 \right] \leq  \sigma^2.
\end{gather*}
<!-- end ass-3 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
These assumptions are standard in traditional stochastic compositional optimization. Some existing multi-level literature~\citep{chen2021solving,Zhang2021MultiLevelCS,TPAMI:2025:Jiang} requires the stronger average smoothness and Lipschitz condition, namely, for each $1\le i\le T$:
\begin{align*}
	\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\left\|f_i(\mathbf{x};\xi)-  f_i(\mathbf{y};\xi)\right\|^2\right] &\leq L_f^2 \left\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\right\|^2,\,
		\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\left\|\nabla f_i(\mathbf{x};\xi)- \nabla f_i(\mathbf{y};\xi)\right\|^2\right]\leq  L_J^2 \left\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\right\|^2.
\end{align*}
However, this assumption is not required in our work.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{L1} 
Set $B_1 \leq \alpha^2 B_0 K$. We can ensure that
\begin{align*}
\Gamma_i \leq \frac{2L_f^2}{\alpha^2 }  \Lambda_{i-1} + \frac{2\alpha   \sigma^2}{B_1};\quad
 \Lambda_i \leq {2\alpha^2L_f^2}\Lambda_{i-1} + \frac{\alpha^2\sigma^2}{B_1}
 + 2\alpha^2 \Gamma_i.
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{L2} 
Let $C_{i+1} = 5+6L_f^2 C_i$ with $C_0=1$. Then
\begin{align*}
\Gamma_i  \leq &C_i \left(\frac{1}{\alpha^2 K}  \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}^{k+1} - \mathbf{x}^{k}\right\|^2\right]  + \frac{ \sigma^2}{B_1} \right);\\
\Lambda_i \leq & C_i  \left(\frac{1}{K}  \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}^{k+1} - \mathbf{x}^{k}\right\|^2\right]  + \frac{\alpha^2 \sigma^2}{B_1} \right).
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
By properly setting the learning rate, we can control the term $\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}^{k+1} - \mathbf{x}^{k}\right\|^2\right]$. Consequently, using a sufficiently large batch size $B_1$ yields a small function-value estimation error.
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{L3}
We have the following guarantee:
    \begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{z}^{k}-\nabla F(\mathbf{x}^{k})\right\|^2\right]
    \leq & \frac{2\alpha }{B_1} T^2(\sigma^2 +L_f^2 )^{T}+\frac{ \sigma^2}{B_1} 4T L_F^2\sum_{i=1}^{T-1} C_i  \\
    & +\left(1+T\sum_{i=1}^{T-1} C_i \right) \frac{4L_F^2}{\alpha^2 K}\sum_{k=1}^{K+1} \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}^{k+1} - \mathbf{x}^{k}\right\|^2\right].
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- head-4: body_md -->
With suitable choices of the learning rate $\eta$ and momentum parameter $\alpha$, we can ensure a small gradient estimation error using a large batch size $B_1$.
<!-- end head-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{T1}
Under Assumptions~\ref{asm:0}, \ref{asm:1}, \ref{asm:stochastic2}, by setting $B_0 = \mathcal{O}(1)$, $B_1 = \mathcal{O}(K)$, $\eta = \mathcal{O}(1)$ and $\alpha =\mathcal{O}(1)$, our MML-v1 algorithm ensures 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla F(\mathbf{x}^k)\right\|\right] \leq \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\right).
\end{align*}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- head-5: body_md -->
To ensure that $\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla F(\mathbf{x}^k)\right\|\right] \leq \epsilon$, the iteration complexity is $K=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ and the overall sample complexity is $B_1 K=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$. 
This matches the lower bound for stochastic single-level optimization under standard smoothness assumptions~\citep{Arjevani2019LowerBF} and is therefore optimal. Notably, this is the first result to obtain optimal $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ sample complexity for multi-level optimization under standard smoothness assumptions.
<!-- end head-5 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{T2}
Under Assumptions~\ref{asm:0}, \ref{asm:1}, \ref{asm:stochastic2}, by setting $B_0=1$, $B_1 = \lfloor K/4 \rfloor$, $\eta = K^{-1/2}$, and $\alpha = 1/2$, our MML-v2 algorithm ensures 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla F(\mathbf{x}^k)\right\|\right] \leq \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\right).
\end{align*}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- head-6: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{T2} provides the same rate while avoiding the use of problem-dependent constants for setting hyperparameters. Note that $\alpha = 1/2$ is not essential to the analysis and can be any positive constant in the range $(0,1)$. A similar normalization technique is also used by \citet{pmlr-v238-hubler24a} in single-level problems. However, our analysis is different from \citet{pmlr-v238-hubler24a}, which analyzes with decreasing $\eta_t$ and increasing $\alpha_t$, and obtains a nearly optimal rate of $\mathcal{O}(K^{-1/4}\log K)$.
<!-- end head-6 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{L1+} 
Set $1 \leq \alpha^2  K$, and we can ensure that
\begin{align*}
	    \Gamma_i \leq &\frac{(4L_f^2+2L_JC +2\sigma^2)}{\alpha}  \Lambda_{i-1} + 3\alpha   \sigma^2;\quad
 \Lambda_i \leq  2\alpha^2\sigma^2  + (6L_f^2+2\sigma^2)\Lambda_{i-1} +  (4\alpha^2)\Gamma_i.
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- head-7: body_md -->
A key improvement over  Lemma~\ref{L1} is the reduction of the factor for $\Lambda_{i-1}$ from ${1}/{\alpha^2}$ to ${1}/{\alpha}$ in the recurrence of $\Gamma_i$. 
This allows us to use a much smaller $\alpha$ to control the term $\alpha \sigma^2$, thereby removing the reliance on a large batch size $B_1$.
We highlight this difference in the following lemma.
\begin{algorithm}[t]
	\caption{MMLFA method}
	\label{alg:2}
	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
	\STATE {\bfseries Input:} parameters $\eta$, $\alpha$, $C$ 
		\FOR{time step $k = 1$ {\bfseries to} $K$}
		\STATE Set $\mathbf{u}^k_0 = \mathbf{x}^k$
  \STATE Compute the function estimator $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_i^k$ according to equation~(\ref{u+})
  \STATE Conduct the clipping operation $\mathbf{u}_i^k = \operatorname{Clip}_{C}[\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_i^k]$
    \STATE Compute the gradient estimator $\mathbf{z}^k$ according to equation~(\ref{z+})
\STATE Update the weight: $\mathbf{x}^{k+1} = \mathbf{x}^k - \eta \mathbf{z}^k $
		\ENDFOR
	\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\begin{lemma}\label{L2+} 
Let $D = 2(7L_f^2+2L_JC +3\sigma^2)$. We obtain:
\begin{align*}
\Gamma_i  \leq & D^i \frac{1}{\alpha K}\sum_{k=1}^K\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}^{k+1} - \mathbf{x}^{k}\right\|^2\right]  + (8 D^{i} +3)\alpha   \sigma^2;\\
\Lambda_i  \leq & D^i \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}^{k+1} - \mathbf{x}^{k}\right\|^2\right] + 8\alpha^2   \sigma^2 D^i.
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}
<!-- end head-7 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{L2+} 
Let $D = 2(7L_f^2+2L_JC +3\sigma^2)$. We obtain:
\begin{align*}
\Gamma_i  \leq & D^i \frac{1}{\alpha K}\sum_{k=1}^K\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}^{k+1} - \mathbf{x}^{k}\right\|^2\right]  + (8 D^{i} +3)\alpha   \sigma^2;\\
\Lambda_i  \leq & D^i \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}^{k+1} - \mathbf{x}^{k}\right\|^2\right] + 8\alpha^2   \sigma^2 D^i.
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- head-8: body_md -->
Compared to Lemma~\ref{L2}, the second term in the function estimation error changes from $\mathcal{O}(\sigma^2/B_1)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\alpha \sigma^2)$, which can be controlled by a small $\alpha$ rather than a large batch size. Also, the factor of the first term is improved from $1/\alpha^2$ to $1/\alpha$, enabling the use of much smaller $\alpha$.
<!-- end head-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{L3+}
Let $D_0 = 2 T^2{(\sigma^2+L_f^2)^T} +4 T L_F^2   \sigma^2(8 D^{T} +3T)$. We have the following guarantee:
    \begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{z}^{k}-\nabla F(\mathbf{x}^{k})\right\|^2\right] \leq D_0 \alpha
     + 4L_F^2\left(1+ T  D^T\right) \frac{1}{\alpha^2K}\sum_{k=1}^{K+1}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathbf{x}^{k+1} - \mathbf{x}^{k}\right\|^2\right].
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- head-9: body_md -->
By properly setting the learning rate $\eta$ and momentum parameter $\alpha$, we ensure a small gradient estimation error with a constant batch size, as $\frac{ \sigma^2}{B_1} 4T L_F^2\sum_{i=1}^{T-1} C_i$ in Lemma~\ref{L3} is eliminated.
<!-- end head-9 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{T1+}
Under Assumptions~\ref{asm:0}, \ref{asm:1}, \ref{asm:stochastic2} and supposing that $\left\|f_i(\mathbf{u}_{i-1}^k)\right\| \leq C$, by setting $\eta = \mathcal{O}(K^{-1/2})$ and $\alpha =\mathcal{O}(K^{-1/2})$, our MMLFA algorithm ensures that:
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla F(\mathbf{x}^k)\right\|\right] \leq \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{K^{1/4}}\right).
\end{align*}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- head-10: body_md -->
To ensure $\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla F(\mathbf{x}^k)\right\|\right] \leq \epsilon$, the sample complexity is $K=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$. This rate matches the previous result while eliminating the need for large batches.
<!-- end head-10 -->
